item.title: EU Funding for SMEs: 7 Open 2026 Calls and How to Qualify
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: EU funding for SMEs in late 2026: 7 open calls from EIC Accelerator to Digital Europe, matched to company size and country, with eligibility steps.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

EU funding for SMEs in late 2026 comes in three main forms. There are direct grants from Brussels-managed programmes (EIC Accelerator, Digital Europe, Horizon Europe, the Single Market Programme), small vouchers such as the EUIPO SME Fund, and EU-backed loans and equity that you get through your local bank or fund. As of 20 October 2026, at least seven calls are open or still reachable for SMEs, with deadlines running from 4 November 2026 to 2 February 2027. To qualify you must meet the official SME definition (fewer than 250 staff, plus ≤€50M turnover or ≤€43M balance sheet), be established in an eligible country, and register a PIC on the Funding & Tenders Portal.

Which option is right for you?

Choose by your stage and what you need the money for. Start with the call that matches your situation, and leave the rest for later.

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to open
Beginner, micro or small firm, needs trade marks or patents protectedEUIPO SME Fund 2026 (Voucher 3 patents is still listed as open)EUIPO SME Fund 2026
Deep-tech startup at TRL 6+ that wants to scaleEIC Accelerator (short proposal now, full proposal at a later cut-off)EIC Accelerator
Cybersecurity or AI company building tools for other SMEsDigital Europe AI4SME call (DIGITAL-ECCC-2027-DEPLOY-CYBER-11-AI4SME)ECCC call announcement
Spin-off or SME holding results from an earlier Horizon/H2020 projectHorizon Europe "Proof of market" (HORIZON-CL4-2027-01-MAT-PROD-49)Knowledge valorisation in WP 2026-2027
University or tech-transfer office"Unlocking academic IP" (MAT-PROD-42) or Venture Builders (MAT-PROD-50)Same knowledge valorisation page
Tight budget, can't co-fund a grantFree advice from the Enterprise Europe Network first, then EU-backed loansaccess2finance
Grant consultant screening calls for clientsFunding & Tenders Portal search filtered to "Open for submission"Funding & Tenders Portal

If none of these match, a new founder can still look at Erasmus for Young Entrepreneurs, a Single Market Programme exchange that places you with a host entrepreneur abroad for 1 to 6 months (European Commission).

What Is EU Funding and How Does It Work for SMEs?

EU funding means grants, equity or guarantees paid from the EU budget. It reaches you either directly from the Commission and its agencies or through national and regional authorities. Which route applies decides where you apply and which rules you follow.

Direct (centralised) management. The Commission or an executive agency publishes calls, evaluates proposals and signs grant agreements. EISMEA, for example, runs the EIC and the Single Market Programme's SME strand. All of these calls sit on one site, the Funding & Tenders Portal. The calls in this guide all use this route, except the EUIPO SME Fund, which runs on its own EUIPO site.

Shared management. Cohesion funds such as the ERDF are spent by national or regional managing authorities, so their calls appear on national portals, not the EU portal. These schemes usually count as state aid. Small amounts often go out under the de minimis rule, which caps aid at €300,000 per undertaking over any three-year rolling period (EUR-Lex summary of Regulation 2023/2831).

Financial instruments. Loans, guarantees and equity under InvestEU never come from Brussels directly. They go through more than 1,000 partner banks, funds and investors that you find via access2finance (Enterprise Europe Brussels).

How a direct grant moves, in order:

  1. The Commission adopts a work programme listing topics and budgets.
  2. Each topic opens as a call on the portal with a fixed deadline (17:00 Brussels time in all the calls below).
  3. You submit through the portal, and independent experts score your proposal against published criteria.
  4. If you are selected, your organisation is validated, a LEAR is appointed, and you sign the grant agreement electronically.

For example, a company applying to the AI4SME cyber call submits by 14 January 2027, and evaluation is planned for February to April 2027 (ECCC call document via FFG). Plan your cash flow around a gap of several months between submission and money.

European Funding for SMEs: Which Programs Apply in 2026?

In late 2026 SMEs have four main programme routes: the EIC Accelerator, Digital Europe, Horizon Europe Cluster 4, and Single Market Programme-linked support. The EUIPO SME Fund covers IP costs on its own track. Each one fits a different stage of innovation.

The 7 calls open or reachable as of 20 October 2026

#Call (ID)Who it suitsMoneyDeadline
1EIC Accelerator Open / ChallengesSingle SMEs/startups, TRL 6–8Grant below €2.5M + equity €1–10MFull-proposal cut-off 4 Nov 2026; short proposals batched monthly
2DIGITAL-ECCC-2027-DEPLOY-CYBER-11-AI4SMECyber/AI firms building tools for SMEs€3–5M per project, 75% rate for SMEs14 Jan 2027
3DIGITAL-ECCC-2027-DEPLOY-CYBER-11-EULEGProjects on EU cybersecurity legislation compliance€20M topic budget14 Jan 2027
4HORIZON-CL4-2027-01-MAT-PROD-49 "Proof of market"Small consortia of spin-offs, startups, SMEsInnovation Action2 Feb 2027
5HORIZON-CL4-2027-01-MAT-PROD-47 Pilot access to Technology InfrastructuresInfrastructure operators serving startups/SMEsCoordination & Support Action2 Feb 2027
6HORIZON-CL4-2027-01-MAT-PROD-42 Unlocking academic IPUniversities, industry, SMEsSee topic page2 Feb 2027
7EUIPO SME Fund 2026Any EU or Ukrainian SMEPatents up to €3,500; plant varieties up to €1,5004 Dec 2026 or until funds run out

Sources: EIC figures from the EIC Accelerator page. Cyber calls from the ECCC announcement and EuroAccess. Horizon topics from the Commission's valorisation page. SME Fund from marchistorici.com and Interpatent. All figures as of October 2026; check the official pages.

What each programme is for

EIC Accelerator. The 2026 budget is €634M: €414M for Accelerator Open and €220M for Challenges (Alien Technology Transfer summary of WP 2026). The minimum equity component went up from €0.5M in 2025 to €1M in 2026 (same source). This route suits companies that want investors and can show a path to scale. It is not for service businesses or projects that are still lab research.

Digital Europe. The programme funds the deployment of digital technology, not research. The ECCC's September 2026 round is worth €96M across seven topics, and €20M of it goes to AI4SME (ECCC). Note that the 10th DIGITAL round, worth about €45.4M, closed on 1 October 2026 (ONE Spain). If you were planning around it, wait for the next round.

Single Market Programme (SMP COSME). The 2026 SME calls have already closed. Tourism SMEs (SMP-COSME-2026-TOURSME-01) closed on 20 May 2026 and Agri-food Biotech Scaling-up on 2 June 2026 (EuroAccess; EISMEA). For the rest of 2026, the SMP mostly reaches SMEs through the Enterprise Europe Network and Erasmus for Young Entrepreneurs, not through new grant calls.

Horizon Europe Cluster 4. These calls usually need a consortium and a Part B written to the scoring criteria. If you are new to that format, read our Horizon Europe Proposal Template Part B: 2026 Scoring Map before drafting.

EU Funding for Small Business: Eligibility by Size and Country

Small-business eligibility depends on two things: the official SME definition and whether your country takes part in the specific programme. Being "small" under your national rules does not count.

The SME thresholds

CategoryStaff headcountTurnoveror Balance sheet
Micro< 10≤ €2M≤ €2M
Small< 50≤ €10M≤ €10M
Medium< 250≤ €50M≤ €43M

Source: Commission SME definition, Recommendation 2003/361. The staff ceiling always applies. Then you need to pass only one of the two financial tests, either turnover or balance sheet (same source).

The Commission has also introduced a "small mid-cap" category for firms that have outgrown SME status (same source). The EIC Accelerator accepts small mid-caps with up to 499 employees, but for the investment component only (EIC).

Country rules differ by programme

Programme / callWho can apply
EIC AcceleratorEU member states and Horizon Europe associated countries. Applicants from other countries can be eligible if they relocate (EIC)
Horizon Europe Cluster 4EU plus associated countries. Canada, New Zealand and South Korea are associated to Pillar II only (alientt.com list; official list: EC country participation PDF)
Digital Europe AI4SMEEU member states, EEA countries (Norway, Iceland, Liechtenstein) and overseas countries and territories (EuroAccess)
EUIPO SME FundSMEs established in the EU and Ukraine (Interpatent)

One consequence trips people up. Cluster 4 is Pillar II, so a Canadian or Korean SME can join a Cluster 4 project. The EIC Accelerator sits in Pillar III, so the same company cannot apply to it from home. The UK, Switzerland, Norway and Ukraine are on the associated list for the whole of Horizon Europe (same sources).

Pitfalls and fixes

  • You count only your own figures. If another company holds a stake in yours, its headcount and finances may have to be added to your figures (Commission). Fix: map your shareholders before you start the SME self-assessment.
  • A venture-backed startup assumes it is automatically an SME. A large corporate shareholder can push you over the thresholds. Fix: read the linked and partner enterprise chapter of the SME User Guide, which is linked from the same Commission page.
  • You rely on an old associated-country list. Association agreements change. Fix: check the official PDF on the call date, not a blog post.

EU Grants for SMEs vs. Loans and Equity: Which Should You Apply For?

Apply for a grant if you have a risky innovation project and can wait months for a decision. Go for an EU-backed loan or guarantee through a local intermediary if you need working capital or investment money sooner.

Direct EU grant (e.g. AI4SME, Horizon)EIC blended financeInvestEU-backed loan/equity
Where to applyFunding & Tenders PortalFunding & Tenders Portal + EIC platformYour bank, fund or VC via access2finance
DilutionNoneEquity €1–10M means investors take a stakeEquity products dilute; loans don't
Co-fundingYes. AI4SME funds 50%, or 75% for SMEsGrant is a lump sum below €2.5MThe intermediary sets the terms
SpeedMonths (AI4SME evaluation Feb–Apr 2027)Short proposal decision in 4–6 weeks, then several stagesSimilar to a normal bank decision
Best forR&D, deployment, consortium projectsScaling deep techEquipment, working capital, expansion

Sources: ECCC call document, EuroAccess, EIC, Enterprise Europe Brussels on access2finance.

How to decide:

  • Choose a grant if the project would not happen without public money and you can pay the uncovered share. At 75% funding, a €4M AI4SME project still leaves you €1M to fund yourself (example calculation).
  • Choose InvestEU-backed finance if the investment is commercially sound but your bank wants more collateral. The EU guarantee is designed to cover exactly that gap (EURA AG).
  • Choose EIC blended finance only if you are comfortable with the EIC Fund becoming a shareholder.

Pitfalls. Don't treat a grant as fast money: with the cyber calls, submission and signature are months apart. Also, access2finance does not lend anything itself. It lists intermediaries, and you apply directly to the institution you pick (Enterprise Europe Brussels).

EU Support for SMEs Beyond Grants: Advisory and Network Services

The cheapest EU support for SMEs is free advice. The Enterprise Europe Network gives partner matchmaking, internationalisation advice and funding guidance at no cost. It is active in more than 60 countries, with around 3,000 experts in more than 600 member organisations (Wikipedia summary; Lithuanian Innovation Centre, an EEN member).

What EEN can do for you:

  • Tell you which calls fit your company and country, including national schemes outside the EU portal.
  • Find consortium partners for Horizon or Digital Europe topics through its partnering database.
  • Review an application idea before you spend weeks writing it.

What it won't do: write your proposal for you. Its advisers are spread thin, so you need to come to them with a specific question.

Other no-cost routes:

  • National Contact Points (NCPs) for Horizon Europe and Digital Europe. They explain topic scope and eligibility. Flanders' NCP, for example, publishes notices about new Digital Europe calls (NCP Flanders).
  • Partner search on each topic page of the Funding & Tenders Portal, under "Partner search announcements".
  • Erasmus for Young Entrepreneurs, for founders and for experienced host entrepreneurs, with EU support towards travel and living costs (European Commission).

How to get EEN help:

  1. Open the Enterprise Europe Network site and find the local contact point for your region.
  2. Send a short email: your sector, headcount, TRL, and the call ID you are considering.
  3. Ask two questions: "Are we eligible?" and "Who else in the network is preparing a proposal on this topic?"

For example, a 30-person Polish cybersecurity firm could ask its local EEN office whether to apply to AI4SME alone or join a consortium. The call allows single applicants but says collaboration can strengthen implementation (EuroAccess).

EU Funding Requirements: Documents and Eligibility Checklist

Every direct EU call requires the same basics: an EU Login account, a 9-digit PIC, an SME self-assessment where SME status matters, and a proposal written to the topic text. Validation documents and a LEAR come later, only if you are selected.

Setup steps on the Funding & Tenders Portal

  1. Create an EU Login. On the portal, click "Login", then "Create an account". Use a work email that more than one person can reach if staff change.
  2. Search for an existing PIC. Under "How to participate" → "Participant Register", search your organisation's legal name first. Duplicate PICs cause delays (Funding & Tenders Online Manual).
  3. Register your organisation. The registration wizard asks for legal name, address, registration country and legal form. You get a 9-digit PIC straight away, but it stays provisional until validated (same source).
  4. Run the SME wizard. If you have no SME self-assessment from the last 2 years, the submission system prompts you to complete one. You enter headcount and financial figures for your last approved accounting period and for any linked enterprises (SME wizard guide; H2020 Online Manual).
  5. Prepare validation documents in advance. If you are selected, the Central Validation Service asks for proof of legal existence and, depending on the entity, financial or legal-status documents (Online Manual).
  6. Appoint a LEAR. Without a LEAR, you cannot update your legal entity data or sign contracts electronically (LEAR appointment).

Call-specific documents

  • Digital Europe AI4SME: Part B of at most 70 pages, plus a mandatory ownership control declaration (EuroAccess).
  • EIC Accelerator short proposal: a 12-page form, a 10-slide pitch deck and a 3-minute video (EIC).
  • EUIPO SME Fund: apply before you pay any IP fees, because paying first loses your right to reimbursement (marchistorici.com).

Common mistakes and fixes

MistakeFix
Registering on the deadline dayGet the PIC at least a week before. It is issued instantly, but EU Login and wizard problems take time
Your SME self-assessment is older than 2 yearsRedo it in the wizard. The system prompts you, but at a bad moment
Paying a trade mark or patent fee before applying for the voucherApply first, pay after approval
Submitting at 16:55 Brussels timeSubmit a draft early. You can resubmit until the deadline, and the latest version counts

How to Check If Your SME Qualifies for a Specific 2026 Call

Open the topic page on the Funding & Tenders Portal, read the "Conditions and documents" section, and check it against your country, legal form, TRL and consortium setup before you write a word. This takes about an hour and can save you weeks of drafting.

Step-by-step check

  1. Go to the Funding & Tenders Portal → "Search Funding & Tenders" → "Calls for proposals".
  2. Under "Submission status", tick "Open for submission". Add "Forthcoming" if you want to plan ahead.
  3. Under "Programme", choose for example "Digital Europe Programme (DIGITAL)" or "Horizon Europe (HORIZON)". Or paste a topic ID such as DIGITAL-ECCC-2027-DEPLOY-CYBER-11-AI4SME into the search box.
  4. On the topic page, read "Topic description" for the expected outcomes and scope. If your project doesn't produce those outcomes, stop here.
  5. Open "Conditions and documents". Check:
  6. Admissibility: page limits (70 for AI4SME).
  7. Eligible countries: EU/EEA for AI4SME; EU plus associated countries for Horizon.
  8. Other eligibility: single applicant allowed or minimum consortium, and any ownership control rules.
  9. Financial and operational capacity: SMEs often have to show their accounts.
  10. Check the "Type of action". An Innovation Action (IA) such as "Proof of market" means near-market work. A Coordination & Support Action (CSA) such as MAT-PROD-47 funds networking and services, not your own product development.
  11. Check TRL fit. The EIC Accelerator expects TRL 6–8 for its innovation activities (EIC).
  12. Check timing against the deadline. Then run steps 1–4 of the requirements checklist above.

Example: three applicants, one afternoon

These are illustrations only.

  • A Norwegian cyber SME with 40 staff. It can apply to AI4SME alone, because the EEA is eligible and single applicants are allowed. Its maximum rate is 75%.
  • A Canadian AI startup. It cannot apply to the EIC Accelerator from Canada because of Pillar III. It could join a Cluster 4 "Proof of market" consortium, because Canada is associated to Pillar II, as long as the topic's own conditions allow it.
  • A Spanish university. "Unlocking academic IP" (MAT-PROD-42) or "Venture Builders Network" (MAT-PROD-50) are a better fit than SME-only instruments. Both close on 2 February 2027 (Commission).

A note on EIC timing

The 4 November 2026 cut-off is for full proposals, and you can only send one after your short proposal is approved. Short-proposal decisions take 4–6 weeks (EIC). If you start today, you will realistically be aiming for a 2027 cut-off. Those dates depend on the next work programme, so confirm them once it is published.

Next steps

Pick one call from the table above and confirm your eligibility for it this week. Leave the drafting until that check is done.

Do it yourself today:

  1. Create your EU Login and search the Participant Register for an existing PIC. Register if there is none.
  2. Run the SME self-assessment wizard with your last approved accounts and any linked-company data.
  3. Open the topic page of your chosen call, read "Conditions and documents", and write down any requirement you don't meet yet.

If you would rather not do it yourself:

  • Enterprise Europe Network and National Contact Points. Free. Good for eligibility checks and partner searches. Not for anyone who wants a proposal written for them, because they don't draft proposals.
  • Private grant consultancies. Most charge a fixed fee, a success fee, or both. There is no official price list, so ask for a written quote (as of October 2026; check each firm's terms). They suit teams with a strong project and no writing capacity. They don't suit very early ideas, because a consultant can't fix weak eligibility or a poor fit with the topic. No consultant can guarantee selection.
  • EIC Business Acceleration Services. Coaching and investor events for companies that already hold EIC funding. Not available before you are selected (EIC).

Related guides on this site:

  • Horizon Europe Proposal Template Part B: 2026 Scoring Map, for anyone drafting a Cluster 4 "Proof of market" or academic IP proposal.

FAQ

What is the EU definition of an SME for funding purposes?

An SME has fewer than 250 staff and either turnover of €50M or less or a balance sheet of €43M or less, under Recommendation 2003/361. Micro firms are under 10 staff and small firms under 50, with lower financial ceilings. Figures from linked or partner enterprises may have to be added to yours (Commission).

Can non-EU companies apply for EU SME funding?

Yes, if their country is associated to the right programme or part of it. Horizon Europe associated countries such as the UK, Switzerland, Norway and Ukraine can access the EIC. Canada and South Korea are associated to Pillar II only. AI4SME is open to the EU and EEA, and the EUIPO SME Fund to the EU and Ukraine.

How much funding can an SME get from the EIC Accelerator?

A grant component below €2.5M as a lump sum, plus optional equity of €1M to €10M. Larger rounds are possible through STEP ScaleUp (EIC). The 2026 Accelerator budget is €634M in total.

Do I need a partner organization to apply for EU SME grants?

Not always. The EIC Accelerator is for single companies, and AI4SME allows single applicants. Many Horizon Europe Innovation Actions need a consortium, so read "Conditions and documents" on the topic page before you look for partners.

Is EU funding for SMEs taxable or does it affect state aid limits?

How a grant is taxed depends on your national law, so ask your accountant how it will be booked. Funding from national or regional schemes, including cohesion funds, often falls under de minimis, which caps aid at €300,000 per undertaking over three rolling years (EUR-Lex). If your project mixes national co-funding with an EU grant, check the state-aid position with your managing authority or national contact point (Irish DETE guidance).

item.title: Horizon Europe Proposal Template Part B: 2026 Scoring Map
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: Horizon Europe proposal template Part B explained section by section, with the 40-page limit, what evaluators score, the 3.1 tables and common mistakes.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

Part B of the Horizon Europe proposal template is the technical description that evaluators read and score. It has three numbered sections, each matching one award criterion: 1. Excellence, 2. Impact and 3. Quality and efficiency of implementation. Under the 2026–2027 Work Programme it is capped at 40 pages for Research and Innovation Actions (RIA) and Innovation Actions (IA), and at 25 pages for Coordination and Support Actions (CSA) (General Annexes 2026–2027). Take the template from the submission system for your topic, write each subsection against the scoring wording below, and upload it as a single PDF.

Which option is right for you?

Choose your starting point based on how much experience you have and how much time you can give it.

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to open
First proposal, no grants officeThe official RIA/IA (or CSA) template plus the evaluation form, read side by sideStandard Application Form (HE RIA/IA)
You write proposals as part of your jobThe evaluation form, used as a checklist for every subsectionEvaluation Form (HE RIA and IA)
Two-stage callOnly sections 1 and 2, within 10 pagesYour topic page on the Funding & Tenders Portal
Lump-sum topicThe lump-sum variant (45 pages for RIA/IA) and its detailed budget tableThe topic's "Topic conditions and documents" area
Small budget, want outside adviceYour National Contact Point (NCP)Horizon Europe NCP portal

The reasoning behind each row: beginners need to learn the scoring language first. Regular writers save the most time by checking every paragraph against the evaluation form. Two-stage first stages are judged only on Excellence and Impact. Lump-sum topics follow different page and budget rules. NCPs are national advisory contacts for Horizon Europe applicants; ask yours what services it offers and on what terms.

What is Part B of the Horizon Europe proposal template?

Part B is the narrative and technical part of the proposal. You upload it as a PDF, and it sits alongside the Part A administrative forms you fill in online. According to the Online Manual, Part A holds the administrative forms and Part B is the "Technical Description", uploaded with any annexes in the submission wizard.

In practice the work splits like this. Part A covers participants, budget figures, the abstract, the ethics and security tables and declarations. Part B covers what you will do, why it matters and how you will deliver it. Evaluators score Part B, and they also check it against Part A. If your budget says a partner has 60 person-months and the Part B effort table says 45, someone will notice.

Here is how a proposal moves through the Portal, using the Online Manual's submission steps:

  1. Create an EU Login account. Every partner organisation needs a PIC (Participant Identification Code), which you get from the Participant Register.
  2. On your topic page, click Start submission to open the submission wizard.
  3. Pre-register the draft proposal, then add the participants and contact persons.
  4. Fill in the Administrative Forms (Part A).
  5. Download the Part B template from inside the submission system. The manual says to use that copy rather than a generic one.
  6. Upload Part B as a PDF, together with any annexes the call requires, then click Submit.
  7. Wait for the acknowledgement of receipt.

Until the deadline you can submit "as many times as you want". Each new version replaces the previous one. To change a submitted proposal, go to My Proposals > View Submitted > Re-edit proposal. This doesn't work for continuously open calls (Online Manual).

For example, a consortium aiming for a May deadline could upload a complete draft PDF a week early. That checks the upload works and protects you against a failed upload on the last day. You then keep replacing it with improved versions.

How is Part B structured section by section?

Part B has three main sections, each with two or three fixed subsections taken straight from the official template. Most supporting information, such as researcher details, ethics and security, now goes in Part A rather than in Part B annexes.

The page counts below are the template's guideline allocations for RIA/IA under the 2026–2027 version, as summarised by Accelopment and Proposia (as of October 2026; check the template inside your call). Only the overall limit is enforced. The per-section figures are guidance.

SectionTitleGuideline pages (RIA/IA)Award criterion it feeds
—Title, acronym, list of participantscounts toward the limit—
1.1Objectives and ambition~4Excellence
1.2Methodology~14Excellence
2.1Project's pathways towards impact~3Impact
2.2Measures to maximise impact (dissemination, exploitation, communication)~3Impact
2.3Summary (key elements of impact)optional since 2026–27Impact
3.1Work plan and resources, with tables 3.1a–3.1h~12 (17 for lump sum)Implementation
3.2Capacity of participants and consortium as a whole~3Implementation

Three changes in the 2026–2027 template are worth knowing if you are reusing an older proposal. Section 2.1 no longer asks for the "scale and significance" of your contribution. Tables 3.1i (other cost categories) and 3.1j (in-kind contributions) have been removed. Section 2.3 is now optional (Future Needs; Accelopment). If you copy text from a 2024 proposal, you will be writing about things that are no longer requested and spending pages you no longer have.

Formatting follows the template's own rules: A4 pages, Times New Roman (or the equivalent named in the template) at a minimum of 11 points, and margins of at least 15 mm (Standard Application Form; GrantForge summary). Tables, figures and references sit inside the sections, so they count toward the limit.

To set up your working document:

  1. Open the template downloaded from the submission system, not a copy a colleague forwarded.
  2. Keep every heading number and title exactly as given. Evaluators look for 1.2, 2.1 and so on by number.
  3. Leave the template's instruction boxes in your working draft, and delete them only in the final PDF.
  4. Next to each heading, paste the matching sentence from the evaluation form. That sentence is what the reviewer will be scoring.

What goes in the Excellence section and what do evaluators score there?

Excellence (section 1) covers your objectives, your ambition beyond the state of the art and your methodology. Evaluators score how clear and pertinent the objectives are, how sound the methodology is and how credible your claims of going beyond the state of the art are.

The RIA/IA evaluation wording, as quoted by GrantForge from the General Annexes, has two parts. The first is the "clarity and pertinence of the project's objectives, and the extent to which the proposed work is ambitious, and goes beyond the state of the art". The second is the soundness of the methodology, including the underlying concepts, models and assumptions, interdisciplinarity, the gender dimension and open science practices.

1.1 Objectives and ambition

Write objectives that someone else could check at the end of the project. A workable pattern is one sentence per objective, saying what will exist, by when, measured how, and in which work package. State your starting and target Technology Readiness Level (TRL) if the topic mentions TRLs. Then describe the state of the art in a few paragraphs, with citations, and say exactly where your work goes further.

Example (illustrative): "O2: Validate the sensor prototype in two operational water utilities, raising it from TRL 4 to TRL 6 by month 30, measured by detection accuracy ≥ 95% against reference lab samples (WP4, D4.3)." Compare that with "advance water monitoring". An evaluator can score the first sentence.

1.2 Methodology

This is the biggest single block, about 14 guideline pages. According to Proposia, the template splits it into the overall approach (~10 pages), links to other R&I projects (~1 page), interdisciplinarity (~0.5), the social sciences and humanities contribution (~0.5), the gender dimension (~1) and open science (~1). Research data management also belongs here.

How to write it:

  1. Start with the concept: the hypothesis or core idea, and the assumptions it depends on.
  2. Walk through the approach in the same order as your work packages, so evaluators can cross-reference 3.1.
  3. Name the methods, datasets, pilot sites and tools you will use, and say why they are suitable.
  4. Give each of the gender, open science and data management subheadings its own short paragraph. If gender is genuinely not relevant, explain why in one or two sentences instead of leaving the heading out.

Pitfalls and fixes

  • Objectives stated as activities ("to organise workshops"). Fix: rewrite each one as a measurable result.
  • A state of the art with no citations, or more than three years old. Fix: cite recent work, including competing EU projects found on CORDIS.
  • Gender dimension mixed up with gender balance in the team. Fix: gender dimension means sex and gender analysis in the research content itself. Team balance is a separate question.

What goes in the Impact section and how is it scored?

Impact (section 2) explains how your results lead to the outcomes and impacts named in the work programme, and how you will disseminate, exploit and communicate them. Evaluators score how credible your pathways are and how suitable your measures to maximise impact are.

Since the 2026–2027 template, section 2.1 asks for the pathway (who benefits, how and why) and no longer asks you to quantify "scale and significance" (Future Needs). That doesn't make numbers useless. A credible pathway often still uses a few well-sourced figures. The difference is that you no longer need to fill a dedicated paragraph with market-size estimates.

For Innovation Actions, Impact carries a weight of 1.5 when proposals are ranked, though not when thresholds are checked (General Annexes, as summarised by GrantForge). In an IA, an extra half-point on Impact is worth more in the ranking than an extra half-point anywhere else.

2.1 Project's pathways towards impact (~3 pages)

  1. Copy the "Expected outcomes" bullets from your topic text and the "expected impacts" from its Destination.
  2. For each outcome, name the result that produces it, the user who will adopt it, and when.
  3. Name the barriers, such as regulation, cost, skills or public acceptance, and say what you will do about each.

2.2 Measures to maximise impact (~3 pages)

Cover the three activities separately:

  • Dissemination: sharing results with people who can use them, for example open-access papers, datasets and standards bodies.
  • Exploitation: who will use which result after the project, through licensing, products, policy uptake or follow-up projects.
  • Communication: reaching the wider public.

Add your intellectual property strategy, meaning who owns which result and how it will be protected.

2.3 Summary (optional)

If you use it, the summary is a one-page canvas linking needs, target groups, outcomes, impacts and your dissemination, exploitation and communication measures. Since the 2026–2027 template it is optional (Accelopment). If you are short of pages, cutting it is reasonable. If an evaluator needs a quick view of a complex pathway, it can help.

Pitfalls and fixes

  • Generic dissemination lists ("website, social media, conferences"). Fix: name the target groups, the channels and a measurable indicator, for example "3 policy briefs to DG ENV and national water regulators by month 24" (illustrative).
  • Impact claims for outcomes the topic never asked for. Fix: tie every claim to the wording of your topic.
  • Exploitation described only for the coordinator. Fix: give each partner a line saying what it will do with which result.

What goes in the Implementation section and what do evaluators check?

Implementation (section 3) covers the work plan, the tables of work packages, deliverables, milestones, risks and effort, and the consortium's capacity. Evaluators check whether the plan can be delivered, whether risks are managed and whether the partners complement one another.

The evaluation wording covers the quality and effectiveness of the work plan, the assessment of risks, whether the effort assigned to each work package is appropriate, and the capacity and expertise of the participants (GrantForge).

3.1 Work plan and resources (~12 pages, 17 for lump sum)

Start with a short overview, a Gantt chart and a PERT diagram showing how the work packages connect. Then fill in the tables. The table structure below is described by Proposia and Accelopment:

TableContentsWhat evaluators check
3.1aList of WPs: number, title, lead, person-months, start/end monthLogical sequence, sensible size
3.1bWP descriptions: objectives, tasks with lead and partner rolesEach task has an owner and an output
3.1cDeliverables: number, name, WP, lead, type, dissemination level, monthDeliverables match the objectives in 1.1
3.1dMilestones: name, WPs, due month, means of verificationVerifiable decision points
3.1eCritical risks: description with likelihood and severity, WPs, mitigationReal risks, specific mitigations
3.1fStaff effort per participant per WPEffort matches the tasks and the Part A budget
3.1gSubcontracting costsJustified and not core tasks
3.1hPurchase costs, with justification where equipment exceeds 15% of personnel costsMajor items explained

How to build it:

  1. Agree the work package list and person-months with all partners before anyone starts writing prose.
  2. Fill in 3.1f first, then check it against the personnel figures each partner enters in the Part A budget.
  3. Number deliverables Dx.y to match their work package, and give every objective in 1.1 at least one deliverable or milestone.
  4. Write 3.1e risks that are specific to this project, such as "pilot utility withdraws". "Delays" is too generic. Pair each risk with a named fallback.

3.2 Capacity of participants and consortium as a whole (~3 pages)

Explain why each partner is in the consortium, what it brings that the others don't, and how the consortium covers the whole value chain the topic implies, for example end users for an IA. Detailed researcher information goes into Part A, so 3.2 should be about how the partners complement each other, not a list of CVs.

Pitfalls and fixes

  • A WP leader with 2 person-months in their own WP. Fix: give WP leaders effort that matches the job of leading.
  • More milestones than decision points. Fix: about 4 to 8 milestones, each with a "means of verification", is easier for evaluators to trust than 20 (an editorial suggestion, not a rule).
  • Using the deleted tables 3.1i or 3.1j from an old template. Fix: start again from the current template.

How do page limits and formatting rules differ by call type (RIA vs IA vs CSA)?

Page limits depend on the type of action and on whether the topic uses lump-sum funding. Anything over the limit is hidden from evaluators after the deadline.

According to the General Annexes 2026–2027, "excess pages will be automatically made invisible". Limits as of October 2026 (check your topic page, because individual topics can set different ones):

Action typeStandard limitLump-sum limit2023–2025 limit (for comparison)Criteria scored
RIA40 pages45 pages45 / 50Excellence, Impact, Implementation
IA40 pages45 pages45 / 50Same; Impact weighted 1.5 for ranking
CSA25 pages28 pages30 / 33Same three criteria, CSA wording
Programme co-fund65 pages——Co-fund criteria
First stage of a two-stage call10 pages——Excellence and Impact only

The 2023–2025 figures come from Accelopment.

Scoring is the same for every action type. Each criterion gets 0–5, with half points allowed. The default threshold is 3 per criterion and 10 overall. In the first stage of a two-stage call only Excellence and Impact are evaluated, and the threshold for each is 4 (HE evaluation briefing; Online Manual PDF). Three scores of exactly 3 add up to 9, which is below the overall threshold.

The CSA template keeps the same three sections, but section 1 is aimed at coordination and support measures rather than research beyond the state of the art (GrantForge). Don't use the RIA template for a CSA topic. Download the variant your topic links to.

Steps to confirm your limit:

  1. Open your topic page on the Portal and scroll to Topic conditions and documents.
  2. Read the type of action (for example "HORIZON-RIA" or "HORIZON-CSA") and check whether lump-sum funding applies.
  3. Check the topic's specific conditions for a different page limit.
  4. Count your pages in the final PDF, including the title page and the participant list.

How do you fill out the mandatory annexes (CVs, ethics, security)?

In Horizon Europe most "annex" content goes into the Part A forms. The ethics self-assessment and the researcher information are entered online, and topic-specific annexes are uploaded only if the call asks for them.

Ethics is handled in two steps in the administrative forms (section 4). First you answer the Ethics Issues Table. Then, for every "Yes", you explain in the Ethics Self-Assessment how you will deal with the issue (UZH Ethics factsheet, April 2025). The Commission's guide "How to complete your ethics self-assessment" is the reference document for this, and it is linked from the Portal's reference documents.

Researcher details are entered in a researchers table in Part A. That table lists only the researchers involved, not administrative staff (RVO template v4.0). Part A also asks each participant for relevant publications, previous projects and significant infrastructure. This is why section 3.2 of Part B should not repeat CVs.

Steps:

  1. Go through the Ethics Issues Table with every partner, not just the coordinator. Human participants, personal data, animals, non-EU countries and dual use are the questions most often answered "Yes".
  2. For each "Yes", write what you will do, who approves it (for example the local ethics committee) and when. Refer to the relevant work package.
  3. Answer the security questions in the same administrative forms. If your topic involves classified information or security-sensitive results, read the topic conditions and the General Annexes for any extra documents required.
  4. For lump-sum topics, upload the detailed budget table the call requires (GrantForge).
  5. Check that the personal data issues ticked in Part A also appear in your data management text in 1.2.

Pitfalls: answering "No" to personal data while the methodology describes interviews; writing ethics text in Part B where nobody reviewing ethics will look for it; and leaving partner-specific issues, such as a non-EU partner's data transfers, out of the self-assessment.

What are the most common mistakes that lower Part B scores?

Most lost points come from going over page limits, vague impact pathways, Part A and Part B figures that don't match, and subsections the topic requires but the proposal leaves out. All of these can be fixed before submission.

The evaluation summary report (ESR) you receive gives comments under each criterion, using the 0–5 descriptors from "Fails" to "Excellent". Score 3 is described as "addresses the criterion well, but a number of shortcomings are present" (GrantForge, quoting the scoring scale). Fixing the mistakes below is how you move from a 3 to a 4.

MistakeEffectFix
Part B over the limitExcess pages are hidden, so a section can disappearCheck the length of the final PDF, not the Word draft
Old template (e.g. 45 pages, tables 3.1i/j)Wasted space, guidance not followedDownload the template again from the submission system
Topic's expected outcomes not addressed one by oneWeak Impact scoreMake a table mapping each outcome to your results in 2.1
Effort in 3.1f ≠ Part A budgetDoubts about feasibilityReconcile the two the day before submission
Generic risksLower Implementation scoreProject-specific risks with named mitigations
Smaller font or tighter spacingBreaks the formatting rulesCut text; keep 11 pt minimum
Gender or open science heading missingWeak spot under ExcellenceOne short paragraph each, or a reasoned "not relevant"

Example (illustrative): a proposal whose 1.1 promises a TRL 6 demonstration, but whose 3.1c lists no demonstration deliverable, invites a comment such as "the link between objectives and work plan is not sufficiently clear". The fix takes one line in the deliverables table.

A final check before you click Submit:

  1. Every heading from the template is present and in the original order.
  2. Every objective links to a WP, a deliverable and a KPI.
  3. Every expected outcome of the topic is mentioned by name in 2.1.
  4. Person-months and costs match Part A.
  5. The PDF opens, is searchable, and is within the page limit.

Next steps

You can do the first round of work today without spending anything.

DIY actions for today:

  1. Open your topic page, note the action type and whether it is lump sum, and write down your page limit (40, 45, 25 or 28).
  2. Download the Part B template through Start submission in the submission system, and save the evaluation form next to it.
  3. Draft table 3.1a (the work package list) and table 3.1f (effort) with your partners before writing any prose.

If you would rather not do it alone: your National Contact Point gives advice and often reviews drafts (as of October 2026; services and terms vary by country, so ask yours what it offers). This suits first-time applicants and SMEs. It is less suited to anyone who needs someone to write the text for them, because NCPs advise rather than write. SMEs can also contact the Enterprise Europe Network, which suits companies looking for partners or innovation support; check the service terms with your local EEN office. Its depth on technical Part B review varies. Private grant consultants will write or edit Part B for a fee. Fee structures vary (day rates, fixed fees, success fees), so ask for a written quote and check their track record on CORDIS. Consultants suit consortia short on time. They are a poor fit if your budget is tight or if the scientific content isn't settled yet, because nobody can write a strong methodology the team hasn't agreed on.

FAQ

Where can I download the official Horizon Europe Part B template?

Get it from inside the Funding & Tenders Portal submission system, after you click Start submission on your topic page. The Online Manual says to use that copy (Online Manual). You can read the general RIA/IA standard application form beforehand, but always submit using your topic's version.

Is Part B submitted as a PDF or filled online?

Part B is uploaded as a PDF in the submission wizard. Part A is filled in online as web forms (Online Manual). You can upload a new PDF as often as you like until the deadline, and the latest version replaces the earlier ones.

What is the page limit for a Horizon Europe RIA proposal?

Under the 2026–2027 Work Programme, a full RIA proposal is limited to 40 pages, or 45 for lump-sum topics. A first-stage proposal in a two-stage call is limited to 10 pages (General Annexes). Individual topics can set a different limit, so check your topic page.

Do I need a different Part B template for different calls?

Yes. RIA/IA, CSA, lump-sum, two-stage and programme-specific actions such as the EIC and MSCA each have their own forms. The Commission publishes them separately, for example the MSCA-PF form and the EIC Accelerator form. Use the one linked from your topic.

What is the difference between Part A and Part B of a Horizon Europe proposal?

Part A is the administrative part: participants, budget, abstract, ethics and security tables, and declarations, all completed online. Part B is the technical description that evaluators score against Excellence, Impact and Implementation. The two must agree on figures such as person-months and costs.
